# Nothobranchius furzeri, an 'instant' fish from an ephemeral habitat

## Authors

- Martin Reichard<sup>1</sup> ([ORCID: 0000-0002-9306-0074](https://orcid.org/0000-0002-9306-0074)) †
- Matej Polačik<sup>1</sup>

### Affiliations

1. Institute of Vertebrate Biology Czech Academy of Sciences Brno Czech Republic

† Corresponding author

## Abstract

The turquoise killifish, Nothobranchius furzeri, is a promising vertebrate model in ageing research and an emerging model organism in genomics, regenerative medicine, developmental biology and ecotoxicology. Its lifestyle is adapted to the ephemeral nature of shallow pools on the African savannah. Its rapid and short active life commences when rains fill the pool: fish hatch, grow rapidly and mature in as few as two weeks, and then reproduce daily until the pool dries out. Its embryos then become inactive, encased in the dry sediment and protected from the harsh environment until the rains return. This invertebrate-like life cycle (short active phase and long developmental arrest) combined with a vertebrate body plan provide the ideal attributes for a laboratory animal.

## Introduction

The African savannah is dotted with ephemeral freshwater pools known as water pans, which form during the rainy season. Killifishes of the genus Nothobranchius, colloquially called annual fishes, have adapted to live in these pools. Popular with specialist aquarium hobbyists for their stunning colouration, most of 75 described species are available in captivity (Neumann, 2008), which is how Nothobranchius furzeri first made its way into research laboratories worldwide. Alessandro Cellerino, a physiologist from Scuola Normale Superiore in Pisa, Italy, was intrigued by an incredibly short-lived population of the annual fish that his friend Stefano Valdesalici bred at home. Experimental investigation of its lifespan revealed that the fish matured after just four weeks, after which their mortality increased sharply from the age of six weeks and all the fish died within 10 weeks (Valdesalici and Cellerino, 2003). The fish of this strain were named GRZ after Gona Re Zhou National Park in Zimbabwe where the fish were originally collected in 1970 (Jubb, 1971). They were later found to live slightly longer as housing conditions developed (Cellerino et al., 2016), though it remains the shortest-lived population of N. furzeri yet recorded. Collection trips to Mozambique and Zimbabwe between 2004 and 2016 assembled a set of populations that vary in lifespan and possess a variable level of inbreeding (Terzibasi et al., 2008; Cellerino et al., 2016; Reichard et al., 2017a).

The remarkably short lifespan of N. furzeri recapitulates the hallmarks of vertebrate ageing (Harel et al., 2015), condensed into few weeks and responsive to pharmacological, dietary and lifestyle interventions (Cellerino et al., 2016). Its genome has been sequenced and assembled (Valenzano et al., 2015; Reichwald et al., 2015), and there are transcriptomes for a number of its tissues (Petzold et al., 2013; Baumgart et al., 2014; Baumgart et al., 2017). Several inbred lines are also available (Hu and Brunet, 2018) and genome-editing techniques are widely adopted to rapidly produce stable transgenic lines too (Harel et al., 2016). With this background, N. furzeri has reached outside the world of ageing research and has become valuable for studies in such disparate branches of investigation as evolutionary genomics (Reichwald et al., 2015), regenerative medicine (Wendler et al., 2015), developmental biology (Hu and Brunet, 2018) and ecotoxicology (Philippe et al., 2018). Here, we explore how our understanding of the natural history of the species makes a key contribution to the development of this species as a laboratory model.

## Natural life cycle and longevity

The life cycle of N. furzeri is adapted to the transient nature of its habitat and is strictly separated into two distinct phases. The first phase starts when fish hatch after their pool is inundated with rainwater and immediately start feeding. Explosive juvenile growth brings them to sexual maturity in as little as two weeks, growing from the initial size of 5 mm to 30–50 mm over that period (Vrtílek et al., 2018a). Growth slows thereafter as resources are diverted to reproduction, but a body size of 75 mm can be reached in males after 10–15 weeks (Blažek et al., 2013; Vrtílek et al., 2018a). Importantly, their growth rate is strongly dependent on population density and food availability; fish in dense populations are typically small and sexually immature at an age of 3–5 weeks, both in the wild and in the laboratory (Graf et al., 2010; Grégoir et al., 2018; Philippe et al., 2018; Vrtílek et al., 2018a). Individual fish vary in growth rates (Blažek et al., 2013), perhaps reflecting variation in personality traits (Thoré et al., 2018). Upon sexual maturity, females lay eggs daily. A typical fecundity of 20–120 eggs per day was estimated in wild populations, with more variation among populations than among females within a sample (Vrtílek and Reichard, 2016; Vrtílek et al., 2018b), seemingly in response to resource availability.

All adult fish die when their pool desiccates, but mortality is strong over the entire lifespan (Vrtílek et al., 2018c). In longer-lasting pools (persisting more than four months), fish often disappear despite the habitat still appearing capable of supporting them. The fish likely succumb to a combination of predation by birds, bouts of extremely high water temperatures, decreased water quality from organic input by visiting animals, low dissolved oxygen levels, exhaustion of resources, and physiological deterioration as a trade-off to rapid juvenile development (Reichard, 2015). While wild-derived, outbred N. furzeri populations have a maximum lifespan (defined as 90% survival at the population level) of 25–42 weeks in captivity (Terzibasi et al., 2008; Tozzini et al., 2013; Blažek et al., 2017), only one of 13 N. furzeri populations monitored in the wild survived beyond the age of 17 weeks and most disappeared at the age of 3–10 weeks as their habitat dried up (Vrtílek et al., 2018c). After desiccation, dry sediment retains the eggs in a dormant state (diapause); an adaptation to the harsh environmental conditions, over the entire dry season that lasts 5–11 months (Cellerino et al., 2016; Vrtílek et al., 2018b).

## Distribution

N. furzeri is distributed in southern Mozambique, with a few populations extending to adjacent parts of southern Zimbabwe, only few kilometres across the border (Figure 1A). Interestingly, the range of N. furzeri lies on a gradient in aridity associated with distance from the coast. Evaporation, the amount of rainfall and its predictability are major environmental factors that vary across that gradient (Terzibasi et al., 2008; Tozzini et al., 2013; Polačik et al., 2018), with the driest and least predictable conditions furthest from the ocean (and at the highest altitude) (Figure 1A). N. furzeri is absent in the wettest region, where another two Nothobranchius species, that otherwise coexist with N. furzeri, maintain viable populations. In contrast, N. furzeri is the most common Nothobranchius species in the dry region, 90–400 km from the coast and 19–220 m above sea level (Reichard et al., 2017a). Two isolated Zimbabwean populations are found even higher, at 325–340 m above sea level. To date, we have located and georeferenced 90 N. furzeri populations over its entire range and their geographic coordinates are accessible at the Figshare repository (doi: 10.6084/m9.figshare.7017167). Our sampling was limited by accessibility from roads and there are many more N. furzeri populations scattered throughout the Mozambican mopane and miombo woodlands and Acacia savannah.

Local pools vary greatly in size and shrink gradually (Vrtílek et al., 2018b) (Figure 2A–B). Environmental conditions in the pool may be harsh; water temperature can fluctuate between 20 and 36°C from early morning to late afternoon (Reichard et al., 2009; Žák et al., 2018). Late in the season (in May), morning water temperature can drop to 15°C. Fine sediment is repeatedly disturbed by cattle (which have functionally replaced the wild African megafauna) (Figure 2C) and partially dissolves in water, producing extremely turbid conditions (Figure 2D). However, in cases when the pool is thickly overgrown with vegetation (Figure 2E) and undisturbed by domestic cattle, the water can be transparent.

## Male colour morphs

Two distinct colour morphs of male N. furzeri occur, often coexisting in the same population (Reichard et al., 2009). The "yellow" morph (Figure 1B) possesses a yellow crescent marking along the outer margin of the caudal fin, outlined by a black margin. "Red" morph males (Figure 1C) have red caudal fins. The extent of colouration on the caudal fin varies widely among wild populations, but the two morphs are clearly discrete (Valenzano et al., 2009; Ng'oma et al., 2014). The black margin of the caudal fin is also present in some populations of red males and exceptionally absent in yellow males. Female colouration is dull and brownish and shows no indication of polymorphism (Figure 1D).

The geographic distribution of the morphs suggests a link between male colouration and adaptations to different habitat conditions. The yellow morph dominates dry, marginal parts of the range, with exclusively yellow males in the driest region of Zimbabwe. Red males dominate populations in the wet part of the range (Figure 1A) (Reichard et al., 2009; Dorn et al., 2011). This contrast is mirrored in the colouration of the most common laboratory strains, with the short-lived GRZ comprising exclusively yellow males while the longer-lived MZM0403 are exclusively red (Cellerino et al., 2016). Interestingly, most natural populations are polymorphic (Figure 1A) and no differences in life history traits between red and yellow males have been established where they coexist. While it is tempting to associate male colouration with adaptation to dry and wet conditions, there is no evidence of any causal link so far.

## Genetic structure

Populations of N. furzeri are divided into two main phylogeographic clades (named Chefu and Limpopo), with limited secondary contact (Terzibasi et al., 2008; Bartáková et al., 2013; Figure 1A). The populations are strongly structured, with rare dispersal between them. The population genetic signature reveals that the Chefu clade has recently experienced dramatic population expansion (Dorn et al., 2011) and demonstrated linkage between populations along the small rivulet basins (Bartáková et al., 2015). Hence, large floods, occurring in exceptionally wet years, are assumed to provide the main mode of dispersal between populations (Reichard, 2015). Surprisingly for a fish, large rivers form boundaries in the distribution of clades and species, including a division of the Limpopo clade to two subclades (Figure 1G) and a boundary between the range of N. furzeri and its sister species, N. kadleci (Bartáková et al., 2015).

## Diet

N. furzeri are opportunistic and generalist predators of small invertebrates. In general, the diet reflects prey availability in particular pools. Small crustaceans (Cladocera, Copepoda, and Ostracoda) typically constitute more than 70% of digested prey, with insect larvae also being a common prey item (Polačik and Reichard, 2010). Backswimmers (nothonectid bugs) are common in the pools but underrepresented in the diet. Chironomid larvae, the most common diet of N. furzeri in the laboratory, are also consumed by wild N. furzeri (Polačik and Reichard, 2010). The diet of N. furzeri differs from the two coexisting species (N. orthonotus and N. pienaari) when prey is abundant though all species resort to any available food of a suitable size when choice is limited (Polačik et al., 2014a). The diet is reflected in the intestinal microbiome and wild N. furzeri populations differ in the microbial composition of their guts (Smith et al., 2017). Interestingly, laboratory fish possess the core microbiota of wild N. furzeri and reconstitution of high microbial diversity in old fish extends their lifespan in the laboratory (Smith et al., 2017).

## Biotic interactions

### Predators

Potential predators include wading and diving birds, such as herons, hammerheads, storks and kingfishers. These birds prey on killifish, tadpoles and, perhaps, larger invertebrates. Large predatory waterbugs are abundant in many pools and readily consume adult killifish in captivity. These sit-and-wait predators may hunt killifish, especially in pools with dense vegetation. Lungfish (Protopterus annectens) commonly coexist with N. furzeri and may also prey on them, though they are not their typical predator (Reichard et al., 2014). The eggs of N. furzeri are likely predated by a range of invertebrates. For instance, freshwater crabs can be abundant in N. furzeri habitats and probably extract killifish eggs from the sediment.

### Parasites

The parasites of wild N. furzeri have been well characterised (Nezhybová et al., 2017). All recorded animal parasites were endoparasites, infecting muscles and internal organs. Perhaps most notably, killifish predominantly hosted intermediate stages of the parasites, forming an important link in the transmission cascade to the final hosts: fish-eating birds. The metacercariae larval stage of parasitic trematodes was by far the most abundant parasite, typically with tens of them infecting the muscle tissue. A surprisingly high diversity of flukes (Trematoda), roundworms (Nematoda) and tapeworms (Cestoda) also reside in N. furzeri muscle, intestine, cerebral and abdominal cavities, gallbladder and gills. It is clear that N. furzeri are challenged by a multitude of infections over their short lifespan and capable of encysting parasites that penetrated their bodies, providing a potential to study their immune responses.

One fluke species deserves particular attention. Larvae of Apatemon sp. infect the cerebral cavity (Nezhybová et al., 2017) and manipulate host behaviour. When attacked by a bird, infected killifish stay close to the water surface, even jumping onto water lily pads and thereby exposing themselves to predators. In contrast, uninfected fish quickly seek refuge when exposed to potential predator attack.

## Reproduction and mating behaviour

All Nothobranchius species are sexually dimorphic (Sedláček et al., 2014). Male colouration and mating behaviour appear strongly sexually selected (Haas, 1976a). Males compete aggressively for access to females and large males are dominant (Polačik and Reichard, 2009). Females express mate choice by approaching a displaying male. Males actively pursue females and may coerce spawning (Polačik and Reichard, 2011). The elaborate male colouration is puzzling, as N. furzeri often live in extremely turbid water where visibility is minimal. Indeed, male colouration fades in turbid water. Courtship is brief; the male approaches a female and stops to perform lateral displays with his unpaired fins extended. A receptive female allows the male to fold her in his dorsal fin and the female lays an egg into the sediment. During oviposition, the pair jerks and the sediment is disturbed. With the aid of stiffened rays of the anal fin, the egg is deposited slightly into the substrate (Passos et al., 2015). Most eggs are found at pool margins (M. Polačik, unpublished data). There is no consistent choice of red or yellow males by individual N. furzeri females (Reichard and Polačik, unpublished data) and mate choice appears to be based on other traits.

Reproduction occurs primarily in the morning. The eggs are ovulated just after sunrise (07:00-08:00) (Haas, 1976b) and by 10:00 some females have already spawned all their ovulated eggs. Most females are spent by 15:00 and a new batch of eggs is ovulated next morning (Vrtílek and Reichard, 2016). Daily fecundity is strongly contingent upon long-term (the effect of body mass: Vrtílek and Reichard, 2016) and short-term (the effect of ration on the preceding day: Vrtílek and Reichard, 2015) access to resources.

## Embryo ecology

The embryonic phase of the N. furzeri life cycle represents the longest but least understood part of the life cycle in the wild. All Nothobranchius populations are limited to pools with a special type of substrate composed of an alkaline swelling clay (Watters, 2009), the physical and chemical properties of which are crucial for the survival of N. furzeri eggs. Annual killifish possess three dormancy stages occurring at defined developmental points (Wourms, 1972) (Box 1). Watters, 2009 proposed a model of natural embryo development of Nothobranchius that links embryo developmental with three phases of incubation conditions (wet, dry and humid) (Box 1).

Large variability in embryo developmental dynamics is a key feature for the long-term persistence of N. furzeri populations in their highly unpredictable environment (Furness, 2016), serving as an effective bet-hedging strategy against false hatching cues, such as insufficient rainfall (Polačik et al., 2017). Erratic rains and mid-season desiccation generate conditions for two (or perhaps even more) generations or cohorts in some years (Reichard et al., 2017b).

Laboratory research in N. furzeri and other annual killifishes has suggested that developmental disparity is achieved through maternal effects, perhaps based on RNA or protein products. Interestingly, embryos of young females tend to develop rapidly while embryos of older females tend to halt development at diapause (Podrabsky et al., 2010; Polačik et al., 2017); a seeming adaptation to the possibility of a second inundation in a single rainy season that the eggs of young females experience more often than the eggs of older females (Polačik et al., 2014b). However, in the wild the beginning and end of diapause, at least in other killifish species, appears to be controlled by environmental factors (Matias and Markofsky, 1978; Podrabsky et al., 2010; Domínguez-Castanedo et al., 2017) and developmental variability may be achieved through habitat heterogeneity rather than intrinsic control. Gradual desiccation and vertical distribution of embryos create a cline of incubation conditions that generate a staggered embryo development.

The course of embryo development has marked impacts on post-hatching lifespan. Rapidly developing embryos produce phenotypes with a rapid post-hatching strategy, typified by a smaller size at hatching but more rapid growth and sexual maturation, and smaller final size and shorter lifespan (Polačik et al., 2014b). It remains to be identified whether embryonic diapause is causally responsible for the limited rapid development later in life, representing one of the outstanding questions to be addressed (Box 2). Intriguingly, in a Neotropical annual killifish, insulin-like growth factor signalling regulates developmental trajectories (Woll and Podrabsky, 2017), representing candidate regulatory pathway for killifish life history.

## Key advantages of N. furzeri for the model species role

The key advantage of N. furzeri as a model species stems from the combination of its rapid post-hatching lifestyle and long phase of embryonic arrest that can be altered by manipulating environmental conditions. Having a model with a vertebrate body plan and invertebrate-like life history and lifespan (i.e. short and rapid active lifespan and dormant stage) is a valuable characteristic beyond the field of ageing research, not least because researchers are often constrained by the duration of grant funding. The arrested stage makes the species ideal for storing and shipping and permits flexible time management when working with this 'instant' fish (Polačik et al., 2016). In addition, given harsh and variable conditions in natural habitats, captive N. furzeri does not require any precise conditions for water quality and housing, perhaps except access to abundant and nutrient rich food (Polačik et al., 2016; Dodzian et al., 2018).

Information on wild N. furzeri populations, and particularly the environmental gradient in its range, have been especially instrumental in explaining differences in lifespan among captive strains (Tozzini et al., 2013; Blažek et al., 2017) and in validating that its rapid life history is not an artefact of the laboratory (Vrtílek et al., 2018a; Vrtílek et al., 2018c). Field studies have also strengthened conclusions on the role of microbiota on ageing (Smith et al., 2017) and genomic insights into the evolution of short lifespan (Valenzano et al., 2015; Reichwald et al., 2015). Formulating a standardised artificial diet that would be readily consumed by captive N. furzeri now appears critical to increase experimental repeatability across laboratories. Detailed understanding of the natural diet of N. furzeri (Polačik and Reichard, 2010; Polačik et al., 2014a) should help the community to accomplish this goal.

## Conclusions

Compared to other fish model systems in biomedical research (e.g. Parichy, 2015), our understanding of the natural history of N. furzeri is substantial (Cellerino et al., 2016). Indeed, N. furzeri may, uniquely, be a model that bridges the interests of ecological and biomedical research (Cellerino et al., 2016). Still, we know relatively little about some features of the natural history of N. furzeri. While some pressing issues are outlined in Box 2, we highlight that the greatest gap in our knowledge of the natural life cycle of N. furzeri is in understanding embryonic development under natural conditions. Data from wild populations demonstrated that high phenotypic plasticity of N. furzeri, manifested in the laboratory by individually disparate growth rates, timing of sexual maturation and fecundity, is natural. While perhaps complicating some experimental designs, it raises a multitude of questions on the underlying mechanisms, from gene expression to individual behaviour (Box 2). With much more to be discovered on the natural history of the species, we anticipate that N. furzeri will continue to be instrumental in showing how conceptual and methodological insights from ecological and biomedical research can be integrated within a single research agenda (Reichard et al., 2015; Cellerino et al., 2016).

Thank you for submitting your article "The Natural History of Model Organisms: Nothobranchius furzeri, an 'instant' fish from an ephemeral habitat" for consideration by eLife. Your article has been reviewed by three peer reviewers, and the evaluation has been overseen by two Features Editors at eLife (Stuart King and Peter Rodgers). The following individuals involved in review of your submission have agreed to reveal their identity: Andrew Furness and Dario Riccardo Valenzano.

After a consultation with the reviewers, the editor has drafted this decision to help you prepare a revised submission.

Summary:

This essay is being considered as part of a series of articles on "The Natural History of Model Organisms" (https://elifesciences.org/collections/8de90445/the-natural-history-of-model-organisms). Each article should explain how our knowledge of the natural history of a model organism has informed recent advances in biology, and how understanding its natural history can influence/advance future studies.

This article summarizes what is known of the natural history of the turquoise killifish (Nothobranchius furzeri), an interesting model organism that is gaining traction in several fields of investigation. The manuscript is compelling, clear and easy to read. However, a number of details should be attended to prior to publication.

The editor may also contact you separately about some editorial or stylistic issues that will need to be addressed.

Essential revisions:

1) The sections in the article provide a comprehensive introduction to the natural history of N. furzeri. However, more should be done to address "how our understanding of the natural history of the species makes a key contribution to its development as a laboratory model" (as stated in the Introduction). Please revise the sections to emphasise how knowledge of N. furzeri's natural history has benefited researchers working with this species in the lab, and/or discoveries in specific fields mentioned in the Introduction. This change would help the article to stand out from other recent (and less-recent) general reviews on N. furzeri as a model system in biology (e.g. Terzibasi et al., 2008; Reichard et al., 2015; Cellerino et al., 2016; Hu et al., 2018).

2) Despite the raising interest about N. furzeri by the scientific community, the reviewers felt it was an overstatement to refer to it as "an established vertebrate model in ageing research" and "the species of choice in […] evolutionary genomics, regenerative medicine, developmental biology and ecotoxicology". This text should be toned down. The revised text should aim to give a more balanced view (i.e. pros and cons) of how the natural history of the species contributes to its usefulness as a model organism. (Brief comparisons with other model organisms, including invertebrates and other vertebrates, could be considered to add wider context or strengthen arguments.)

3) Some of the cited work on killifish diapause and reproduction is from species besides N. furzeri; yet the way the references are cited does not make this clear to a reader unfamiliar with the system. Please include a 'disclaimer' somewhere in the text to indicate that what is known about diapause/development is drawn from studies of other related annual killifish, and although many aspects seem to be highly congruent among species, it remains to be determined whether the same applies to N. furzeri specifically.

4) The main text mentions that little is known about the development in the wild. As such, please consider including at least one or two question about the developmental pathways of N. furzeri embryos in the wild into the "Outstanding questions" in Box 2.

5) The paper currently includes 60 references, 28 of which are directly from the two authors. Though the authors have majorly contributed to the development of N. furzeri as a biomedical and ecological system, they should consider if all these citations are needed and if other articles have been missed from the reference list.

results.result: N. furzeri is established as a promising model in aging research and an emerging model in genomics, regenerative medicine, developmental biology, and ecotoxicology.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C5 are supported by the manuscript's introduction and are consistent with the cited literature establishing N. furzeri's role across multiple research domains. These are well-documented applications of the species as a model organism.

results.result: N. furzeri has a biphasic life cycle adapted to ephemeral pools, with rapid maturation (as few as two weeks), daily reproduction until pool desiccation, and embryonic dormancy in dry sediment.
results.evaluation: Claims C6-C9, C32-C34 describe the fundamental life cycle characteristics of N. furzeri. These are well-supported by the manuscript text and are consistent with the species' adaptation to ephemeral habitats. The claims are internally consistent and represent established knowledge about the species.

results.result: The genus Nothobranchius contains 75 described species, most of which are available in captivity.
results.evaluation: Claims C10-C11 are supported by citation to Neumann, 2008. This represents established taxonomic knowledge about the genus and is appropriately cited.

results.result: The GRZ strain of N. furzeri, collected from Zimbabwe in 1970, exhibits extremely short lifespan with maturation at 4 weeks, sharp mortality increase at 6 weeks, and death by 10 weeks, though slightly longer under improved housing conditions. It remains the shortest-lived population recorded.
results.evaluation: Claims C12-C17 are well-supported by citations to Valdesalici and Cellerino, 2003; Jubb, 1971; and Cellerino et al., 2016. The lifespan data are specific and appropriately cited. The comparative statement about it being the shortest-lived population is supported by the manuscript's assessment.

results.result: Collection trips between 2004-2016 assembled N. furzeri populations that vary in lifespan and inbreeding levels.
results.evaluation: Claims C18-C19 are supported by multiple citations (Terzibasi et al., 2008; Cellerino et al., 2016; Reichard et al., 2017a) documenting field collection efforts and population characterization.

results.result: N. furzeri's short lifespan recapitulates vertebrate aging hallmarks and is responsive to pharmacological, dietary, and lifestyle interventions.
results.evaluation: Claims C20-C23 are supported by citations to Harel et al., 2015 and Cellerino et al., 2016. These establish the species' value as an aging model and its responsiveness to interventions, which are key features for experimental manipulation.

results.result: N. furzeri has sequenced genome, tissue transcriptomes, inbred lines, and widely adopted genome-editing techniques for producing transgenic lines.
results.evaluation: Claims C24-C27 are supported by multiple citations documenting genomic resources (Valenzano et al., 2015; Reichwald et al., 2015), transcriptomes (Petzold et al., 2013; Baumgart et al., 2014, 2017), inbred lines (Hu and Brunet, 2018), and genome editing (Harel et al., 2016). These represent established molecular resources.

results.result: N. furzeri has become valuable for studies in evolutionary genomics, regenerative medicine, developmental biology, and ecotoxicology.
results.evaluation: Claims C28-C31 are supported by citations to specific studies in each field (Reichwald et al., 2015; Wendler et al., 2015; Hu and Brunet, 2018; Philippe et al., 2018), demonstrating the species' expanding utility beyond aging research.

results.result: N. furzeri exhibits explosive juvenile growth reaching sexual maturity in as little as two weeks (growing from 5mm to 30-50mm), with growth slowing after maturity as resources are diverted to reproduction, but males can reach 75mm after 10-15 weeks.
results.evaluation: Claims C35-C38 are supported by citations to Vrtílek et al., 2018a and Blažek et al., 2013. The growth data are specific and quantitative, with appropriate citations. The inference about resource diversion (C37) is reasonable given the life history context.

results.result: Growth rate in N. furzeri is strongly dependent on population density and food availability, with fish in dense populations typically small and sexually immature at 3-5 weeks in both wild and laboratory settings.
results.evaluation: Claims C39-C41 are supported by multiple citations (Graf et al., 2010; Grégoir et al., 2018; Philippe et al., 2018; Vrtílek et al., 2018a) documenting density-dependent growth effects in both natural and laboratory conditions.

results.result: Individual N. furzeri vary in growth rates, perhaps reflecting variation in personality traits.
results.evaluation: Claim C42 is supported by citation to Blažek et al., 2013, but C43 is speculative (indicated by 'perhaps') and cites Thoré et al., 2018. The link between growth rate variation and personality traits requires further validation and represents a hypothesis rather than an established result.

results.result: Female N. furzeri lay eggs daily upon maturity with typical fecundity of 20-120 eggs/day in wild populations, showing more variation among populations than within populations, seemingly in response to resource availability.
results.evaluation: Claims C44-C46 are supported by citations to Vrtílek and Reichard, 2016 and Vrtílek et al., 2018b with specific quantitative data. Claim C47 is an inference (indicated by 'seemingly') but is reasonable given the documented variation patterns and ecological context.

results.result: All adult N. furzeri die when pools desiccate, with strong mortality throughout lifespan. In longer-lasting pools (>4 months), fish often disappear despite apparently suitable habitat, likely due to multiple stressors including predation, temperature extremes, water quality decline, low oxygen, resource exhaustion, and physiological deterioration.
results.evaluation: Claims C48-C50 are supported by citation to Vrtílek et al., 2018c. Claim C51 is an inference (indicated by 'likely') supported by citation to Reichard, 2015, proposing multiple contributing factors to mortality. The inference is reasonable given the harsh environmental conditions described.

results.result: Wild-derived, outbred N. furzeri populations have maximum lifespan of 25-42 weeks in captivity (defined as 90% survival), but in the wild only 1 of 13 monitored populations survived beyond 17 weeks, with most disappearing at 3-10 weeks as habitats dried.
results.evaluation: Claims C52-C55 are supported by multiple citations (Terzibasi et al., 2008; Tozzini et al., 2013; Blažek et al., 2017; Vrtílek et al., 2018c). The definition of maximum lifespan (C53) is clearly stated, and the contrast between captive and wild lifespans is well-documented with specific quantitative data.

results.result: After desiccation, N. furzeri eggs enter dormant diapause in dry sediment over a dry season lasting 5-11 months.
results.evaluation: Claims C56-C57 are supported by citations to Cellerino et al., 2016 and Vrtílek et al., 2018b, documenting the diapause adaptation and dry season duration with specific timeframes.

results.result: N. furzeri is distributed in southern Mozambique with a few populations extending into southern Zimbabwe, lying on an aridity gradient associated with distance from coast, with evaporation, rainfall amount and predictability varying across the gradient, and driest/least predictable conditions furthest from ocean at highest altitude.
results.evaluation: Claims C58-C62 are supported by text, Figure 1A, and citations to Terzibasi et al., 2008; Tozzini et al., 2013; Polačik et al., 2018. The geographic distribution and environmental gradient are well-documented with both visual (Figure 1A) and cited evidence.

results.result: N. furzeri is absent in the wettest region where two other Nothobranchius species maintain populations, but is the most common species in the dry region (90-400 km from coast, 19-220 m elevation), with two isolated Zimbabwean populations at 325-340 m elevation.
results.evaluation: Claims C63-C66 are supported by text and citation to Reichard et al., 2017a. The distribution pattern along the aridity gradient is specific and quantitative, showing ecological niche differentiation among Nothobranchius species.

results.result: 90 N. furzeri populations have been georeferenced across the species' range with coordinates accessible at Figshare repository, though many more populations likely exist beyond those sampled due to accessibility limitations.
results.evaluation: Claims C67-C68 are supported by specific data availability statement with DOI. Claim C69 is a reasonable inference about sampling limitations. The georeferenced dataset represents a significant field survey effort.

results.result: N. furzeri pools experience harsh environmental conditions with water temperature fluctuating 20-36°C daily (dropping to 15°C late season), fine sediment repeatedly disturbed by cattle (which have functionally replaced wild megafauna) producing extremely turbid conditions, though water can be transparent in vegetated pools undisturbed by cattle.
results.evaluation: Claims C70-C75 are supported by citations (Reichard et al., 2009; Žák et al., 2018) and Figures 2C-E. The temperature data are specific and quantitative. The inference about cattle replacing megafauna (C73) is reasonable given the ecological context. The contrast between turbid and clear water conditions is documented with visual evidence.

results.result: Two distinct male color morphs exist in N. furzeri (yellow with yellow crescent on caudal fin outlined in black; red with red caudal fins), often coexisting in populations. Caudal fin coloration extent varies among populations but morphs are clearly discrete. Black margin is present in some red males and exceptionally absent in yellow males. Females are dull brownish with no polymorphism.
results.evaluation: Claims C76-C85 are supported by citations (Reichard et al., 2009; Valenzano et al., 2009; Ng'oma et al., 2014) and Figures 1B-D. The morphological descriptions are specific and documented with visual evidence. The discrete nature of morphs despite variation is well-established.

results.result: Geographic distribution of color morphs suggests a link between male coloration and habitat adaptation, with yellow morphs dominating dry regions (exclusively in driest Zimbabwe areas) and red males dominating wet regions. This pattern is mirrored in laboratory strains (short-lived GRZ is yellow; longer-lived MZM0403 is red). However, most natural populations are polymorphic, no life history differences exist between morphs where they coexist, and there is no evidence of causal links between coloration and environmental adaptation.
results.evaluation: Claims C86-C89 are supported by citations and Figure 1A showing geographic patterns. Claims C90-C91 about laboratory strains are supported by Cellerino et al., 2016. However, claims C92-C94 indicate that despite suggestive patterns, the causal relationship remains unestablished. The result presents a correlation without mechanistic understanding, making the adaptive significance uncertain.

results.result: N. furzeri populations are divided into two main phylogeographic clades (Chefu and Limpopo) with limited secondary contact and strong population structure with rare dispersal. The Chefu clade experienced recent dramatic population expansion and shows linkage along rivulet basins. Large floods in exceptionally wet years are assumed to provide the main dispersal mode.
results.evaluation: Claims C95-C99 are supported by citations (Terzibasi et al., 2008; Bartáková et al., 2013, 2015; Dorn et al., 2011) and Figure 1A. Claim C100 is an inference (indicated by 'assumed') supported by Reichard, 2015, which is reasonable given the population genetic patterns and habitat characteristics.

results.result: Large rivers form boundaries in the distribution of N. furzeri clades and species, dividing the Limpopo clade into two subclades and forming a boundary between N. furzeri and its sister species N. kadleci.
results.evaluation: Claims C101-C103 are supported by citation to Bartáková et al., 2015 and Figure 1G. The observation that rivers act as barriers for this fish species is noted as surprising and is well-documented phylogeographically.

results.result: N. furzeri are opportunistic generalist predators with diet reflecting prey availability. Small crustaceans constitute >70% of prey, with insect larvae also common. Backswimmers are underrepresented despite being common. Chironomid larvae (most common laboratory diet) are also consumed in the wild. Diet differs from coexisting species when prey is abundant, but all species use any suitable food when choice is limited.
results.evaluation: Claims C104-C112 are supported by citations to Polačik and Reichard, 2010 and Polačik et al., 2014a. The dietary data are quantitative (>70% crustaceans) and include comparative information with other species. The feeding ecology is well-characterized.

results.result: Diet is reflected in intestinal microbiome, with wild N. furzeri populations differing in gut microbial composition. Laboratory fish possess the core microbiota of wild fish, and reconstitution of high microbial diversity in old fish extends laboratory lifespan.
results.evaluation: Claims C113-C116 are supported by citation to Smith et al., 2017. The microbiome-lifespan connection (C116) is particularly significant as it demonstrates a functional link between gut microbiota and aging, with experimental evidence of lifespan extension.

results.result: Potential predators include wading/diving birds (herons, hammerheads, storks, kingfishers) that prey on killifish, tadpoles, and perhaps larger invertebrates. Large predatory waterbugs are abundant and readily consume adult killifish in captivity, and may hunt them in vegetated pools. Lungfish commonly coexist and may prey on killifish though not typically. Eggs are likely predated by invertebrates including freshwater crabs that probably extract eggs from sediment.
results.evaluation: Claims C117, C119-C120, C122 are supported by observations and citation to Reichard et al., 2014. However, claims C118, C121, C123, C124, C126 contain speculation (indicated by 'perhaps', 'may', 'likely', 'probably') about predation that lacks direct observational or experimental evidence. The predator community is described but predation rates and impacts are not quantified.

results.result: Wild N. furzeri parasites are well-characterized, with all recorded animal parasites being endoparasites infecting muscles and internal organs. Killifish predominantly host intermediate parasite stages, forming an important transmission link to fish-eating birds. Metacercariae (trematode larvae) are the most abundant parasite (tens per fish in muscle). High diversity of flukes, roundworms, and tapeworms reside in various tissues. Fish are challenged by multiple infections and can encyst penetrating parasites.
results.evaluation: Claims C127-C134 are supported by citation to Nezhybová et al., 2017. The parasitological data are specific and quantitative (tens of metacercariae), documenting parasite diversity, abundance, tissue distribution, and the fish's role in parasite transmission cycles.

results.result: Apatemon sp. larvae infect the cerebral cavity and manipulate host behavior. When attacked by birds, infected killifish stay near the surface and jump onto lily pads, exposing themselves to predators, while uninfected fish quickly seek refuge.
results.evaluation: Claims C135-C138 are supported by citation to Nezhybová et al., 2017. The behavioral manipulation by parasites is specific and represents a clear example of parasite-induced behavioral changes that increase transmission to final hosts (birds).

results.result: All Nothobranchius species are sexually dimorphic with male coloration and mating behavior appearing strongly sexually selected. Males compete aggressively for females with large males dominant. Females express mate choice by approaching displaying males. Males actively pursue females and may coerce spawning.
results.evaluation: Claims C139-C144 are supported by citations (Sedláček et al., 2014; Haas, 1976a; Polačik and Reichard, 2009, 2011). The mating system is well-characterized with both male-male competition and female choice documented.

results.result: Elaborate male coloration is puzzling as N. furzeri often live in extremely turbid water with minimal visibility. Male coloration fades in turbid water.
results.evaluation: Claims C145-C146 present an apparent paradox between elaborate coloration and turbid habitat conditions. The phenotypic plasticity of coloration (C146) in response to turbidity is documented, though the adaptive significance remains unclear. This represents an interesting unresolved question about sexual selection in this system.

results.result: Courtship is brief with males approaching females and performing lateral displays with extended unpaired fins. Receptive females allow males to fold them in dorsal fins. During oviposition, the pair jerks and disturbs sediment. With stiffened anal fin rays, eggs are deposited slightly into substrate. Most eggs are found at pool margins.
results.evaluation: Claims C147-C151 are supported by citation to Passos et al., 2015 describing spawning behavior. Claim C152 is supported by unpublished data from M. Polačik. The spawning behavior is described in detail with specific morphological and behavioral components.

results.result: There is no consistent choice of red or yellow males by individual females, and mate choice appears to be based on other traits.
results.evaluation: Claims C153-C154 are based on unpublished data from Reichard and Polačik. While this addresses the color morph question, the lack of peer-reviewed publication and the speculative nature of C154 (indicated by 'appears') make this result uncertain. The alternative traits driving mate choice are not identified.

results.result: Reproduction occurs primarily in the morning. Eggs are ovulated just after sunrise (07:00-08:00), with some females spawning all eggs by 10:00. Most females are spent by 15:00, and a new batch is ovulated next morning.
results.evaluation: Claims C155-C159 are supported by citations to Haas, 1976b and Vrtílek and Reichard, 2016. The reproductive timing is specific and quantitative, documenting the daily reproductive cycle with precise timeframes.

results.result: Daily fecundity is strongly contingent upon both long-term (body mass effect) and short-term (ration on preceding day) access to resources.
results.evaluation: Claims C160-C161 are supported by citations to Vrtílek and Reichard, 2015, 2016. The resource-fecundity relationship is documented at both temporal scales, showing plasticity in reproductive output.

results.result: The embryonic phase represents the longest but least understood part of the life cycle in the wild. All Nothobranchius populations are limited to pools with alkaline swelling clay substrate, whose physical and chemical properties are crucial for egg survival. Annual killifish possess three dormancy stages at defined developmental points. Watters (2009) proposed a model linking embryo development with three incubation phases (wet, dry, humid).
results.evaluation: Claims C162-C166 are supported by citations to Watters, 2009 and Wourms, 1972. The substrate specificity (C163-C164) and developmental model (C165-C166) are well-documented. Claim C162 acknowledges a knowledge gap, which is appropriate.

results.result: Large variability in embryo developmental dynamics is key for population persistence in unpredictable environments, serving as a bet-hedging strategy against false hatching cues like insufficient rainfall. Erratic rains and mid-season desiccation can generate conditions for two or perhaps more generations/cohorts in some years.
results.evaluation: Claims C167-C168 are supported by citations to Furness, 2016 and Polačik et al., 2017, establishing the adaptive significance of developmental variability. Claim C169 is supported by Reichard et al., 2017b with some speculation ('perhaps') about multiple cohorts, which is reasonable given the environmental variability.

results.result: Laboratory research suggests developmental disparity is achieved through maternal effects, perhaps based on RNA or protein products. Embryos of young females tend to develop rapidly while embryos of older females tend to halt at diapause, a seeming adaptation to the possibility of second inundation that young females' eggs experience more often.
results.evaluation: Claims C171-C172 are supported by citations to Podrabsky et al., 2010 and Polačik et al., 2017. However, claims C170 and C173 are speculative (indicated by 'perhaps' and 'seeming') about the molecular mechanisms and adaptive significance. The maternal age effect is documented but the mechanistic basis and causal relationship to environmental conditions require further validation.

results.result: In the wild, diapause beginning and end in killifish appears controlled by environmental factors, and developmental variability may be achieved through habitat heterogeneity rather than intrinsic control. Gradual desiccation and vertical embryo distribution create a cline of incubation conditions generating staggered development.
results.evaluation: Claim C174 is supported by citations to other killifish species (Matias and Markofsky, 1978; Podrabsky et al., 2010; Domínguez-Castanedo et al., 2017) but with inference ('appears'). Claims C175-C176 are speculative ('may') about mechanisms in N. furzeri specifically. The environmental control hypothesis is reasonable but requires direct validation in N. furzeri under natural conditions.

results.result: Embryo development course has marked impacts on post-hatching lifespan. Rapidly developing embryos produce phenotypes with rapid post-hatching strategy (smaller at hatching, more rapid growth/maturation, smaller final size, shorter lifespan). Whether embryonic diapause is causally responsible for limited rapid development later remains to be identified.
results.evaluation: Claims C177-C178 are supported by citation to Polačik et al., 2014b, documenting the developmental programming effects on life history. Claim C179 appropriately identifies the causal mechanism as an outstanding question, acknowledging the limitation of current knowledge.

results.result: In a Neotropical annual killifish, insulin-like growth factor signaling regulates developmental trajectories, representing a candidate regulatory pathway for killifish life history.
results.evaluation: Claim C180 is supported by citation to Woll and Podrabsky, 2017 for a different killifish species. Claim C181 extrapolates this to N. furzeri as a 'candidate pathway' which is speculative. While the inference is reasonable given phylogenetic relatedness, direct evidence in N. furzeri is needed.

results.result: The key advantage of N. furzeri as a model stems from combining rapid post-hatching lifestyle with long embryonic arrest that can be manipulated. Having a vertebrate body plan with invertebrate-like life history is valuable beyond aging research. The arrested stage makes the species ideal for storing/shipping and permits flexible time management. Captive fish do not require precise water quality/housing conditions, perhaps except abundant nutrient-rich food.
results.evaluation: Claims C182-C185 are supported by citation to Polačik et al., 2016. Claim C186 is supported by citations to Polačik et al., 2016 and Dodzian et al., 2018. These claims appropriately assess the practical advantages of the species as a laboratory model.

results.result: Information on wild populations and environmental gradients has been instrumental in explaining lifespan differences among captive strains and validating that rapid life history is not a laboratory artifact. Field studies have strengthened conclusions on microbiota's role in aging and genomic insights into short lifespan evolution.
results.evaluation: Claims C187-C190 are supported by multiple citations (Tozzini et al., 2013; Blažek et al., 2017; Vrtílek et al., 2018a,c; Smith et al., 2017; Valenzano et al., 2015; Reichwald et al., 2015). These demonstrate how field studies have validated and strengthened laboratory findings.

results.result: Formulating a standardized artificial diet readily consumed by captive N. furzeri appears critical for experimental repeatability across laboratories. Detailed understanding of natural diet should help accomplish this goal.
results.evaluation: Claims C191-C192 are assessments of research needs (indicated by 'appears' and 'should') supported by citations to Polačik and Reichard, 2010 and Polačik et al., 2014a. While the need is reasonable and natural diet is characterized, the development and validation of a standardized diet remains to be accomplished.

results.result: Compared to other fish model systems in biomedical research, understanding of N. furzeri natural history is substantial. N. furzeri may uniquely bridge the interests of ecological and biomedical research.
results.evaluation: Claims C193-C194 are supported by citation to Cellerino et al., 2016. While C194 contains speculation ('may'), the assessment is reasonable given the documented integration of field and laboratory studies presented throughout the manuscript.

results.result: The greatest knowledge gap is understanding embryonic development under natural conditions. Data from wild populations demonstrated that high phenotypic plasticity (disparate growth rates, maturation timing, fecundity) is natural. N. furzeri is anticipated to continue being instrumental in integrating ecological and biomedical research insights.
results.evaluation: Claims C195-C196 appropriately assess current knowledge and gaps. Claim C197 is a forward-looking statement (indicated by 'anticipate') supported by citations to Reichard et al., 2015 and Cellerino et al., 2016, which is reasonable given the demonstrated integration throughout the manuscript.
